explanations.explanation: Rezin, king of Aram, and Pekah, king of Israel, do march on Jerusalem together. But the text says “…he could not overpower the city.” (Isaiah 7:1) Two kings, one big march, and Jerusalem is still standing. That's a lot of walking for no city.

Right, they march up together, but they can't finish the job. Rezin, king of Aram, and Pekah, king of Israel, come to wage war against Jerusalem. The text says “…he could not overpower the city.” (Isaiah 7:1) That's a whole lot of marching for a city that still isn't overpowered.

explanations.answer: Tremble like trees in the wind
explanations.explanation: That's the picture the text gives. When the news reaches the house of David, the hearts of Ahaz, king of Judah, and his people trembled “…like trees in the forest shaken by the wind.” (Isaiah 7:2) A whole forest, getting shaken. I think that's what bad news feels like in the chest.

explanations.answer: Stand tall like cedars on a hill
explanations.explanation: Cedars standing tall sounds brave, but that's not what happens here. The text says the hearts of Ahaz and his people trembled “…like trees in the forest shaken by the wind.” (Isaiah 7:2) These trees are doing the shaking, not the standing. I think a few knees were knocking too.

explanations.answer: Burn like fire in dry brush
explanations.explanation: Fire does show up in this passage, but not in their hearts. The text says Ahaz and his people trembled “…like trees in the forest shaken by the wind.” (Isaiah 7:2) The fire comes in verse 4, where the LORD uses it to describe the two kings. So you've got the right neighborhood, just a different address.

I get why you'd think it, with two kings coming and a king shaking. But the LORD sends Isaiah the prophet with a different message: “Calm down and be quiet. Do not be afraid or disheartened…” (Isaiah 4:4) No army talk at all. Me, I'd have been pacing circles around the bakery, and the message is to calm down.

Right, there's no march in this message. The LORD tells Isaiah the prophet to say to Ahaz, “Calm down and be quiet. Do not be afraid or disheartened…” (Isaiah 7:4) A shaking king hears about calming down, not gathering troops. That's a whole different kind of plan.

That's the LORD's picture of Rezin, king of Aram, and the son of Remaliah, king of Israel. Verse 4 says, “…these two smoldering stubs of firewood…” (Isaiah 7:4) A smoldering stub is barely holding a glow. I think it's a very small thing to lose sleep over.

explanations.answer: Two roaring lions in the hills
explanations.explanation: Lions would make anyone nervous, but that's not the LORD's picture. He calls the two kings “…two smoldering stubs of firewood…” (Isaiah 7:4) Nobody ever got chased through the hills by a stub of firewood, I can tell you that. A stub just sits there and smolders.

Mighty oaks would be a heavy comparison, but the text goes the other way. The LORD calls the two kings “…two smoldering stubs of firewood…” (Isaiah 7:4) That's firewood that's already mostly burned down. Oaks stand for years, and stubs are nearly done.

That's the name in the plot. Aram and Ephraim say, “Then we can install the son of Tabeal over it as king.” (Isaiah 7:6) The Bible tells us nothing more about him, so I won't make anything up. He's the name on their plan, and that's all we have.

The son of Remaliah is Pekah, king of Israel, and he's named among those who plotted. The plan says, “Then we can install the son of Tabeal over it as king.” (Isaiah 7:6) That's a different name than his. So the pick is the son of Tabeal.

The son of Jotham is Ahaz, the king of Judah right now. He's the one the plot is aimed at, so he's not the pick. The plan says, “Then we can install the son of Tabeal over it as king.” (Isaiah 7:6) Ahaz is the king they want out, not in.

That's exactly what He says. The Lord GOD tells Ahaz, “It will not arise; it will not happen.” (Isaiah 7:7) The two kings made a plan, and the Lord GOD answered it in one short sentence. Their plan doesn't stand a chance.
It's the other way around. The Lord GOD says of their plan, “It will not arise; it will not happen.” (Isaiah 7:7) Aram and Ephraim made a plan, and that's the Lord GOD's answer to it. A plain no.

Shattered is the word. God says, “Within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered as a people.” (Isaiah 7:8) That's a big word for a big change. And notice God puts a number on it: sixty-five years.

Blessed sounds nice, but it's not what God says. He says, “Within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered as a people.” (Isaiah 7:8) Ephraim is one of the two plotting against Judah. So this verse is no blessing for them.

Multiplied would mean more of them, and God says the opposite. “Within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered as a people.” (Isaiah 7:8) Shattered means broken apart, not added up. That's a heavy word.

God says it plainly: “If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.” (Isaiah 7:9) After all that talk about kings and plots, God lands on faith. That's what He tells Ahaz to stand firm in. And I'd say that's worth writing on the flour jar.

An army is the first thing most of us would grab. But God doesn't mention one. He says, “If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.” (Isaiah 7:9) The standing God asks for is faith, not troops.

Walls are a natural guess when a city is under threat. But God doesn't say a word about them here. He says, “If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.” (Isaiah 7:9) Me, I'd have been out there checking those walls twice, but the warning is about faith.

A sign is exactly what the LORD offers. He tells Ahaz, “Ask for a sign from the LORD your God…” (Isaiah 7:11) A sign is something Ahaz could see with his own eyes. The LORD is the one inviting him to ask.

A blessing sounds nice, but that's not the word. The LORD says, “Ask for a sign from the LORD your God…” (Isaiah 7:11) A sign is something you can point to and say, there it is. That's what's being offered to Ahaz.

Reward is a fun guess. But the verse says, “Ask for a sign from the LORD your God…” (Isaiah 7:11) The offer is a sign, something Ahaz can see. If I got to pick a reward, I'd ask for extra chocolate chips.

I can see why you'd think Ahaz says yes. The LORD offers a sign from the depths of Sheol or the heights of heaven. But Ahaz answers, “I will not ask; I will not test the LORD.” (Isaiah 7:12) The door is wide open and he stays outside.

Right, Ahaz turns the offer down. The LORD says to ask for a sign, and Ahaz replies, “I will not ask; I will not test the LORD.” (Isaiah 7:12) The text doesn't say why he answers that way, and I won't guess. All we know is he says no to a sign.

explanations.answer: He asks if David's house will try God's patience
explanations.explanation: That's how Isaiah answers. He says, “Hear now, O house of David! Is it not enough to try the patience of men? Will you try the patience of my God as well?” (Isaiah 7:13) Isaiah the prophet is speaking to the house of David, which is the family of kings Ahaz belongs to. His answer is two pointed questions.

explanations.answer: He praises Ahaz for honoring the LORD's name
explanations.explanation: Ahaz's words might sound respectful, but Isaiah doesn't hand out praise. He says, “Is it not enough to try the patience of men? Will you try the patience of my God as well?” (Isaiah 7:13) That's a question with some weight behind it. Isaiah is not patting him on the back.

explanations.answer: He agrees and walks away without a word
explanations.explanation: Isaiah the prophet has plenty to say. He answers, “Hear now, O house of David! Is it not enough to try the patience of men? Will you try the patience of my God as well?” (Isaiah 7:13) No quiet exit here. The man is just getting started.

That's what Isaiah says. “Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign…” (Isaiah 7:14) Ahaz had said, “I will not ask; I will not test the LORD.” (Isaiah 7:12) Ahaz said no to asking, and the Lord Himself gives one anyway.

Isaiah is the one delivering the message, so it's a fair guess. But he says, “Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign…” (Isaiah 7:14) Isaiah is the messenger. The sign comes from the Lord Himself.

Priests aren't mentioned anywhere in this passage. Isaiah says, “Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign…” (Isaiah 7:14) Isaiah names the Lord Himself as the giver. That's the answer to look for.

That's what Isaiah says. “For before the boy knows enough to reject evil and choose good, the land of the two kings you dread will be laid waste.” (Isaiah 7:16) Ahaz has been dreading those two kings, and Isaiah tells him their land will be laid waste. That's a promise with a timeline attached.

It's actually true, and I think the verse sounds almost too good for a shaking king. Isaiah says, “For before the boy knows enough to reject evil and choose good, the land of the two kings you dread will be laid waste.” (Isaiah 7:16) The kings Ahaz dreads are the ones whose land gets laid waste. The news was meant for Ahaz.

explanations.answer: The king of Judah and his people
explanations.explanation: That's who Isaiah is talking to. He says, “The LORD will bring on you and on your people and on the house of your father a time unlike any since the day Ephraim separated from Judah…” (Isaiah 7:17) Ahaz is the king of Judah, so "you" means him. His people and the house of his father are in it too.

explanations.answer: The king of Moab and his people
explanations.explanation: Moab isn't in this passage at all. Isaiah says, “The LORD will bring on you and on your people and on the house of your father…” (Isaiah 7:17) He's talking to Ahaz, the king of Judah. So the time unlike any is coming for Judah.

explanations.answer: The king of Edom and his people
explanations.explanation: Edom doesn't appear in this passage. Isaiah says the LORD will bring this time “…on you and on your people and on the house of your father…” (Isaiah 7:17) The "you" is Ahaz, king of Judah. Edom is nowhere on the guest list.

I'd guess a whistle is easy to ignore, but not this one. The text says the LORD whistles to the flies and the bees, and “…they will all come…” (Isaiah 7:19) They don't stay at the Nile or in Assyria. They come and settle in the ravines, the thornbushes and the watering holes.

The whistle works. The LORD whistles to the flies at the farthest streams of the Nile and to the bees in Assyria, and “…they will all come and settle…” (Isaiah 7:19) Every last one of them shows up. That's a pretty obedient swarm.

The beard is the third thing. The Lord uses the razor “…to shave your head and the hair of your legs, and to remove your beard as well.” (Isaiah 7:20) The razor is the king of Assyria, hired from beyond the Euphrates. It leaves nothing out.

A razor doesn't take sandals, and the text doesn't mention them. It says the Lord will use it “…to shave your head and the hair of your legs, and to remove your beard as well.” (Isaiah 7:20) It's all about hair, from the head to the legs to the beard.

The text doesn't mention a robe. It says the Lord uses the razor “…to shave your head and the hair of your legs, and to remove your beard as well.” (Isaiah 7:20) The razor is the king of Assyria, and the beard goes with the rest.

I get the picture of one cow and two sheep and not much to show for it. But the text says the opposite. “…from the abundance of milk they give, he will eat curds…” (Isaiah 7:22) The man has an abundance of milk. He's eating, and he's eating well.
Right, there's plenty. The text says, “…from the abundance of milk they give, he will eat curds…” (Isaiah 7:22) One young cow and two sheep, and still an abundance. The man has plenty to eat.

explanations.answer: All who remain in the land
explanations.explanation: That's who it is. The text says, “for all who remain in the land will eat curds and honey.” (Isaiah 7:22) The verse doesn't pick favorites. Everyone who remains is at the table.
The king and his officials aren't named here. The text says, “for all who remain in the land will eat curds and honey.” (Isaiah 7:22) It's everyone left in the land. No special table for anybody.

The verse doesn't name Assyria's soldiers. The text says, “for all who remain in the land will eat curds and honey.” (Isaiah 7:22) The ones named are all who remain in the land. That's the answer to look for.

That's what's there. “…in every place that had a thousand vines worth a thousand shekels of silver, only briers and thorns will be found.” (Isaiah 7:23) Those vines were worth a lot of silver. And now it's only briers and thorns.

Wheat would be a happy ending, but the verse doesn't give one. It says, “…only briers and thorns will be found.” (Isaiah 7:23) This was land that had a thousand vines worth a thousand shekels of silver. Now there's nothing ripe about it.

Olive trees would be a nice replacement, but that's not what grows. The verse says, “…only briers and thorns will be found.” (Isaiah 7:23) The place had a thousand vines worth a thousand shekels of silver. Now the only things standing there are prickly.

That's what the text says. “Men will go there with bow and arrow, for the land will be covered with briers and thorns.” (Isaiah 7:24) Bow and arrow, and briers and thorns everywhere. The land has gone from tended to overgrown.

It's actually true. “Men will go there with bow and arrow, for the land will be covered with briers and thorns.” (Isaiah 7:24) I'd have guessed they'd bring a pair of gloves, but the text says bow and arrow. The land has gone from tended to overgrown.

That's where the hills end up. The verse says, “they will become places for oxen to graze and sheep to trample.” (Isaiah 7:25) These are hills once tilled by the hoe. Now it's animals doing the walking.

Towns full of people would be the opposite of this verse. The text says people will no longer traverse those hills for fear of the briers and thorns. “they will become places for oxen to graze and sheep to trample.” (Isaiah 7:25) The hills are given to animals, not people.
Grapes aren't in this verse. The hills were once tilled by the hoe, but now “they will become places for oxen to graze and sheep to trample.” (Isaiah 7:25) No grapes in the picture. Just hooves.
